The first thing that comes is the sound of rain on a tin roof in a house I’ve never actually lived in but somehow remember perfectly. It’s 3:17 a.m. in that memory, and the power is out. A single candle is burning on the kitchen table, throwing long shadows that look like tired people leaning against the walls, waiting for something that never arrives. I’m sitting there with a cup of coffee that’s gone cold, watching the flame dance like it’s trying to tell me a secret in a language I almost understand.

There’s a peculiar freedom in having exactly one thousand words and no assignment except to let them spill. It feels like standing at the edge of a cliff with a parachute you’re not sure will open, but the view is so stupidly beautiful you jump anyway. So here we are, falling.

I’ve been thinking lately about how every person is a walking archive of abandoned futures. All the versions of ourselves we killed off because they were inconvenient or embarrassing or too brave. The girl who wanted to be a marine biologist until she realized she gets seasick. The boy who practiced guitar until his fingers bled, then quietly put it in the closet when no one came to his shows. The woman who almost ran away to Berlin at twenty-three with nothing but a backpack and a broken heart. They’re all still in there, rattling around like marbles in a jar. Sometimes at night I can hear them whispering to each other.

My grandmother used to say that memory is a muscle. The more you use it, the stronger it gets. But she also said if you flex it too hard you might pull something that can never be put back right. I think she was right on both counts. I remember the exact smell of her hands—coffee grounds and Pond’s cold cream—and the way she could make the word “sugar” sound like both an endearment and a warning. I remember less useful things too. The exact shade of blue of a sweater I wore the day my first dog died. The sound my father made when he laughed at his own bad jokes. The way my mother’s voice would get very small when she was most angry.

There’s a Japanese concept called *mono no aware*—the gentle sadness at the transience of things. I think about it constantly. The way cherry blossoms are most beautiful right before they fall. The way a song can wreck you precisely because it ends. The way every hello contains the shape of its eventual goodbye, like a shadow you haven’t met yet but already recognize.

I’ve been trying to be kinder to my younger selves. The ones who stayed up all night reading books under the covers with a flashlight. The ones who cried in bathroom stalls. The ones who said the wrong thing at the exact wrong moment and then replayed it for years. They were doing their best with the information they had. They were terrified and hopeful and trying so hard it hurts to remember. I want to reach back through time and tell them: *It’s okay. The world is bigger than this moment. Your heart is not a mistake.*

Sometimes I wonder what the world would look like if we could see each other’s abandoned futures floating around us like ghosts. Would we be gentler? Would we recognize the boy who almost became a poet in the tired accountant who snaps at the barista? Would we see the almost-painter in our difficult boss? Would we understand that everyone is haunted by the lives they didn’t live?

There’s a bird outside my window right now that sounds like it’s gargling marbles. It’s infuriating and perfect. Life is like that. Full of things that are simultaneously ridiculous and sacred. The way we cry at commercials about dogs but ignore the homeless veteran on the corner. The way we spend hours curating our online personas while forgetting how to talk to the people in the next room. The way we’re all convinced we’re the main character while secretly suspecting we might be an NPC.

I keep a small notebook where I write down questions I don’t have answers for. Some of them are stupid. Some of them keep me up at night. “What if the universe is just God’s way of talking to Himself?” “Why does the smell of cut grass make me want to cry?” “If I could send one memory back to my eight-year-old self, what would it be?” (It would be the feeling of my grandmother’s hands, I think. The certainty that someone in this world knew exactly how to love me.)

The rain in my head has stopped. The candle is still burning though. The shadows have gotten comfortable, leaning there like old friends who don’t need to speak. I think that’s what this is really about—learning how to sit in the dark with yourself without panicking. Learning that silence isn’t emptiness. That the spaces between things are where the meaning lives.

We’re all just stories we tell ourselves until we become them. The trick is to tell better stories. Kinder ones. Braver ones. Stories that leave room for the possibility that you might still surprise yourself.

I’m at 847 words now. The bird is still gargling. My coffee is still cold. The candle is still burning.

And I am still here.

Still falling.

Still writing.

Still becoming.

The last 153 words are for you, whoever you are, reading this at whatever time it is in your life. I hope you’re being gentle with yourself today. I hope you remember that the abandoned futures aren’t failures—they’re proof that you had the courage to choose. I hope you know that somewhere, in some version of reality, the marine biologist and the guitarist and the girl who ran away to Berlin are all cheering for you. They’re saying: *Keep going. The story isn’t over.*

The candle flickers.

The rain starts again.

And the words run out exactly on time.
